analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal for employers to permanently replace striking workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee, and got no hearing or vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, an employer can hire permanent replacements for workers on strike, meaning strikers risk losing their jobs forever. This bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act to make that practice an unfair labor practice. Employers could still hire temporary workers during a strike, but could not threaten or offer permanent jobs to strikebreakers. The bill was introduced in July 1989 and never advanced past a subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Striking workers gain real leverage: they could walk a picket line without risking permanent dismissal, which strengthens unions' ability to bargain. Workers at companies contemplating a strike would also gain from the deterrent, since employers could no longer credibly threaten to replace the entire workforce.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to hire, threaten to hire, or agree to hire permanent replacements for employees on strike, for either economic strikes or unfair labor practice strikes [S2][S3].
Applies from the first day of a strike, so employers could no longer use the threat of permanent replacement as a bargaining weapon at the outset of a dispute [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially large unionized companies, lose a powerful tool for ending strikes on their terms: the ability to permanently replace a striking workforce. That could raise the cost of labor disputes and make employers bargain harder against union demands.

drawbacks.text: The bill tilts bargaining power toward unions: a striking workforce that cannot be permanently replaced can impose prolonged production shutdowns, and employers and their allies argue this raises costs that flow into prices and discourages investment.

The ban covers both economic strikes and unfair labor practice strikes, removing the distinction current law draws between employers who have violated the law and those simply resisting a contract demand [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives striking workers genuine job security, which is real and immediate. The honest cost is that strikes could last longer and become more disruptive for employers and the economy, and the leverage shift in negotiations would be substantial. Whether that tradeoff is good policy is the core debate over banning permanent replacements; the bill does not attempt any middle ground such as a sunset or arbitration requirement.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee and its Labor-Management Relations Subcommittee until the Congress ended, never reaching a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 21, 1989, by Rep. Foglietta with eight cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced [S5].
On August 24, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill was never reported out of committee, never scheduled for a floor vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — particularly large unionized companies — are better off, because they kept their legal ability to permanently replace striking workers. Workers lost the chance to gain protection for exercising their right to strike.

for.name: Rep. Thomas Foglietta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban the hiring of permanent strikebreakers.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill; it was referred to the full committee on July 21, 1989, and to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations on August 24, 1989, and never reported back.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; with only 8 of 257 House Democrats signing on, the bill never had the breadth to move, and no Republican supported it in the record.

industries.note: The bill would strip employers of their ability to permanently replace a striking workforce, the practice the bill targets. Their gain from the bill's failure is workers' continued exposure to permanent replacement.
Businesses that supply permanent strikebreakers would lose that market under the ban; the bill's death preserved it.
